title: Ops SLA & data flow interview - Marathon Ledger
next_steps: Send residency diagram + hosted vs dedicated comparison (Alex)
Schedule 1:1 with Crypto/legal for KMS key escrow questions (Renee to propose times)
action_items: Alex - email hosted/dedicated network diagram by 2025-06-26

transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2025-06-24
- Time: 14:00 PDT
- Duration: 53 minutes (approx)
- Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Daniel Price (Marathon Ledger - Head Infra), Renee Tang (Marathon - Compliance), Omar Velasquez (Platform)

Summary:
Short intro call to map Marathon Ledger's data residency and audit requirements and to surface whether Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, or Private makes the most sense. Main concerns: PHI-like customer identifiers in some flows, strict financial data retention rules, need for tenant isolation, KMS controls and key residency, and retention/forwarding of inference logs.

Topics covered:
- current infra and where model inputs/outputs flow
- examples of data classified as regulated vs non-regulated
- acceptable hosting modes and escalation path for Private deployment
- audit log retention windows and redaction needs
- KMS/HSM and key escrow concerns

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intro — I'm Alex, AE on the Redwood side, Priya is our solutions engineer. Um, we wanted to run through your residency and compliance constraints, okay?
[00:12] Daniel: Yeah, hi Alex, thanks. We'll mostly be focused on flow and evidence. I'm Dan, I run infra. Renee will cover compliance.
[00:18] Renee: Hi all. I, uh, want to be clear up front — we have a mix of financial transactions and some user-submitted docs that could be PII. There may be HIPAA-like controls for certain partner data.
[00:32] Priya: Thanks Renee. Can you — at a high level — tell us where the model inputs come from today? Are they coming from a backend queue, from user uploads, from partner APIs?
[00:42] Omar: Mostly backend API gateway -> internal auth layer -> message bus. A handful are file uploads processed by an ETL before the request hits inference.
[00:50] Daniel: Also, for some billing ops, we enrich with third-party lookup that returns banking identifiers — those are considered regulated.
[01:02] Priya: Got it. So two flows — streaming request with small token payloads, and bulk inference from ETL. For the bulk ETL we usually recommend Dedicated or Private since you can control batch windows and network egress. For streaming, Hosted can work but we need to ensure no PHI tokens end up in logs.
[01:20] Renee: The big question is auditability. We need cryptographic evidence of key use, and also a clear path for logs that must never leave EU datacenters for certain customers.
[01:30] Alex: Sure. Redwood supports region pinning for hosted — we can route inference to eu-west-1 regions only for those tenants — however, Hosted still means control plane traces may be in our control plane depending on config. Dedicated gives you network isolation and you can opt for "private control plane" with our Private offering.
[01:48] Daniel: Can you clarify "private control plane"? Our security folks are very specific: no telemetry leaves our VPC except what we explicitly allow.
[01:56] Priya: Private Control Plane in our usage means the control plane services are deployed into the customer's VPC or on-prem environment — breathing room for the RBAC and SSO flows. Logging can be configured to avoid egress to Redwood-managed buckets. In practice, we also offer an audit log stream to kinesis/sqs or customer SIEM.
[02:15] Renee: Kinesis is good. Do you support envelope encryption with customer-managed keys? We cannot have Redwood hold the raw keys for certain data classes.
[02:24] Priya: Yes, we support KMS integration — both cloud KMS and an HSM-backed provider. You can pass keys for at-rest encryption; for private deployments, keys can remain in your HSM. For Hosted, we offer CMEK but for high-regulated workloads we usually recommend Dedicated with customer KMS or Private.
[02:42] Omar: If we go Dedicated, what is the boundary for logs? Specifically, model token logs — are those written anywhere searchable by Redwood ops? We need to be able to redact tokens and ensure minimal retention.
[02:53] Alex: Great question. By default, Redwood collects minimal telemetry for SLOs and billing. Token-level logs are optional. For Dedicated, you can turn off token capture and enable metric-only telemetry. If you need token logs for troubleshooting, we have redaction hooks and ephemeral KV cache dumps that can be directed to your storage with short TTLs.
[03:16] Renee: Short TTLs are fine but we need immutability/evidence for access — who accessed which key, when. Does Redwood provide signed audit trails?
[03:24] Priya: We can emit signed audit events to your audit collector. For Private deployment we can produce locally-signed logs under your CA. For Hosted we provide audit logs that include actor, timestamp, and operation — but there are nuances for cryptographic signing, we can run that by our security engineering team.
[03:41] Daniel: Ok. What about data residency for indexing/embedding stores? We plan to store embeddings for semantic search. Those must live in our EU region for EU customers.
[03:51] Priya: Embedding stores can be configured to your region. If you're using Hosted and choose EU-only, the embedding store and inference will be pinned. For additional isolation, Dedicated clusters can be deployed in your cloud account and your storage.
[04:05] Omar: There's also the question of model weights. Are weights ever replicated across regions? We have concerns about model artifacts containing caches that could leak sensitive tokens.
[04:15] Alex: We use model variants; weights are not considered user data but we do have memory of temporary KV caches for attention states. Those caches are ephemeral and we can ensure they're stored only on local SSDs that are wiped. For Private, you control the machines entirely.
[04:34] Renee: On the evidence side — in audits we need to show non-repudiation of access to data and keys. We also need to know the retention policy for logs and a deletion process with certs.
[04:44] Priya: We provide retention policies configurable per tenant. Deletion operations produce a deletion certificate (a signed event) you can archive. For Hosted we keep a default retention but we can negotiate shorter windows for enterprise customers.
[04:58] Daniel: Is there an option for runbooks and playbooks for legal holds? Sometimes legal will request a hold on certain data for an investigation.
[05:06] Alex: Yes — we have a legal hold feature that freezes retention for specified objects and marks them for separate audit. For Private/Dedicated you can fully control the mechanism; for Hosted it's a supported enterprise feature with designated support flows.
[05:22] Renee: We also need SSO integration and SCIM for provisioning — our auditors ask about orphan accounts and role separation.
[05:29] Priya: Full SAML/SSO with SCIM is supported across all deployment modes. RBAC is granular — you can define roles that only access metrics, not token logs, etc.
[05:41] Omar: Performance question briefly — if we pin to EU only and use Dedicated, what's the expected latency hit for our EU region users versus using Hosted global endpoints?
[05:52] Priya: Latency will usually be lower if you deploy Dedicated close to your users. The tradeoff is throughput and cost; Hosted uses our global routing and optimized kernel selection which gives slightly lower cold-start behavior, but Dedicated in-region usually beats cross-region Hosted routing for median p95. We can run bench with your sample workload.
[06:10] Daniel: Benchmarks would be great. We'll need an SLA number though — our ops requires <200ms p95 for auth-path generative completions at 256 tokens.
[06:20] Alex: We can commit to working toward that with Dedicated and pinned model variants — we have historical p95 numbers in our performance deck, but we'll schedule a dedicated benchmark session with Priya's help.
[06:33] Renee: Back to compliance — what exact certifications do you publish? SOC2 Type II yes, ISO?
[06:40] Priya: SOC2 Type II, ISO 27001, and we publish a HIPAA whitepaper outlining controls and responsabilité. We do not produce HIPAA certification but we provide a BAA and controls mapping.
[06:55] Renee: For BAA we'll need more specific controls around PHI minimization in inference logs.
[07:02] Alex: Understood. We can map which logs are tokenized, give redaction examples, and provide the BAAs typical customers sign.
[07:12] Daniel: A question about fallback routing — during a regional outage, will requests failover to other regions? For some EU customers we cannot fail across to US.
[07:22] Priya: You can configure strict region-only routing and disable cross-region fallback. If you require hard geofencing, Dedicated/Private is the recommended path. Hosted has fallback but region-locking is configurable at tenant-level for enterprise accounts.
[07:38] Omar: About telemetry — can we get token-level metrics without the tokens themselves — e.g., counts of redactions, redacted token lengths?
[07:47] Priya: Yes, aggregated telemetry is available. We also support hooks that return only hash digests for sample tokens for debugging; hashes can be salted to avoid reversibility.
[07:58] Renee: That helps. Also, for any third-party enrichment (the banking lookup), does Redwood touch that data, or can we chain enrich before sending to Redwood to avoid raw PII?
[08:08] Daniel: Our preference is to do enrichment in-house and send labeled/hashed identifiers to inference.
[08:14] Alex: That's a good pattern. For privacy-first setups, best practice is to tokenize or hash upstream, or do deterministic hashing with your salt, then pass to Redwood. For cases you need full text search, you can keep embeddings locally and only surface secure IDs to the model.
[08:30] Omar: Ok so next steps, from a technical POV we want a bench, a residency diagram, and the compliance docs. From compliance we want the BAA and redaction workflows.
[08:39] Alex: We'll send: (1) a network/service diagram showing Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private flows, (2) SOC2 + HIPAA scoping doc, (3) a proposed bench plan with sample payloads.
[08:49] Renee: And please indicate which artifacts would require an NDA or extra legal review.
[08:53] Alex: Will do.
[09:00] Daniel: Two last quick items: escrow of keys in multi-region — we need to know if keys can be replicated but only accessible from EU.
[09:08] Priya: Key replication is controlled by your KMS. For cloud KMS, replication can be region-limited. For HSM-based Private, keys stay on-prem. We'll pull our crypto team into the follow-up for precise architecture.
[09:21] Renee: Thanks. Also curious about data deletion proof — you mentioned deletion certificates, is that an automated signed event?
[09:28] Alex: Yes, it's an automated event with a signature. We'll provide a sample certificate format.
[09:34] Omar: Great. Any immediate blockers?
[09:37] Daniel: None yet. Cost story is the other factor but we'll review after we see the dedicated vs hosted delta.
[09:44] Alex: Understood. We'll include rough delta estimates in the follow-up.

Action items (captured in call):
- Alex to send residency diagram and hosted/dedicated comparison by 2025-06-26.
- Priya to share SOC2 + HIPAA scoping docs by 2025-06-27.
- Renee to surface Marathon's data classification doc by 2025-07-02.
- Schedule benchmark session (Priya & Omar) - target week of 2025-07-07.

Closing notes:
[09:50] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and propose times for the benchmark. Appreciate the clarity on the constraints — this helps route whether Hosted can satisfy EU-only workloads or whether Dedicated/Private is necessary.
[09:59] Renee: Thanks. Please cc our legal on any BAA drafts.
[10:03] Alex: Will do. Bye all.

End of transcript.
